title: RL-driven eviction prototype lab notes
content:
Context and goal:

This is a working lab notebook for the prototype RL-based eviction policy we spun up in the staging cluster (s-x3-gpu-pool) in Q4–Q5 2025. Primary goal: evaluate whether a lightweight, per-host incremental RL agent can improve useful-reuse rate and reduce pageback IO compared to the tuned LRU/priority hybrid we currently run. Secondary goals: measure stability (oscillation), memory bandwidth impact, and SLO tail effects (p95/p99 token latency).

Why RL?
- Static heuristics (age+freq scoring) are simple but brittle across changing customer mixes and seqlen distributions.
- We want an online policy able to adapt to workload drift (seqlen shifts, new prompt templates) without frequent manual retuning.
- Keep model small: policy ~1k parameters, observation vector per candidate includes recency, local reuse count, per-tenant score, seqlen histogram bucket, and last-evict-pressure.

High-level design decisions:
- Agent lives in the host-level cache coordinator, runs at eviction decision points only (no per-token runtime inference). This keeps overhead low and avoids GPU usage.
- Actions: choose eviction candidate set order (we limited to top-K candidates by lightweight admission filter).
- Reward: composite of (a) +1 for a subsequent reuse within 4 seconds (heuristic), (b) -2 if eviction causes a pageback read within 200ms, (c) small negative for choosing very large-span entries (to reduce bandwidth pressure). Reward shaping tuned incrementally.
- Training mode: on-policy incremental online learning with experience replay limited to last 10k decisions. We used a tiny policy-gradient update every 500 decisions; learning rate annealed during pilot.

Data collection and instrumentation:
- Added decision telemetry: candidate feature vector, chosen candidate id (hashed), reward observed, time to next reuse or spill, host mem pressure at decision time. Logged to synthetic-s3/staging/evictor-rl-stream/ for analysis.
- Added microbench route: synthetic workloads generator (synth-evictor) that can replay trace segments with controlled seqlen distribution, hotset churn, and multi-tenant mixing.
- Collected GPU and NIC bandwidth counters to check for unexpected network/DMA amplification during pagebacks.

Benchmarks run (short summary):
1) Baseline trace (steady hotset, seqlen 96): run length 1 hour, mixed tenancies (10 tennants).
   - Baseline (LRU-priority): reuse rate (within 4s) = 72.3%, p99 token latency = 161 ms, pageback reads = 2.2 IOPS/sec averaged, avg memory bandwidth 62 GB/s.
   - RL prototype (after warmup 10k decisions): reuse rate = 78.9% (+9.2%), p99 latency = 150 ms (-6.8%), pageback reads = 1.6 IOPS/sec (-27%).
2) Surge workload (hotkey spike every 90s, bursty arrivals): 30 min runs
   - Baseline: reuse rate 58.5%, p99 token latency 312 ms, pageback reads spike to 11 IOPS/sec during bursts, memory bandwidth burst up to 92 GB/s.
   - RL: reuse 66.1% (+13%), p99 295 ms (-5.5%), but observed instability: oscillation in candidate churn causing transient bandwidth spikes (peak 105 GB/s) on two hosts.
3) Long-tail churn (new hotset items introduced gradually): 4 hour run
   - Baseline: reuse 64.0%, p99 190 ms, steady pagebacks 3.1 IOPS/sec
   - RL: reuse 72.4% (+13.1%), p99 182 ms (-4.2%), improved amortized throughput but higher variance in host-level cache occupancy (stddev +18%).

Key observations and hypotheses:
- RL improves useful reuse consistently in steady and slow drift scenarios. The agent learns to favor recently reused prefixes more aggressively than LRU while demoting large, low-reuse entries (win for bandwidth).
- In bursty/periodic surges, agent exhibits oscillatory behavior: it rapidly evicts overlapping working-sets between bursts and then re-pulls them, causing higher peak memory bandwidth and pageback amplification. Hypothesis: reward window (4s) is too short; agent optimizes for short-term reuse and ignores the cost of re-fetching after a short lull.
- Per-host learning leads to model fragmentation: separate agents converge to different local optima. This is OK for heterogenous loads but complicates debugging and rollout (we saw some hosts converge on overly aggressive eviction which hurt per-tenant tail SLOs).
- The admission filter (bloom-based) is still a good gate; removing it increased agent search space and worsened stability.

Microbench metrics correlating oscillation:
- Oscillation episodes align with high per-host cache recovery rate (>1500 evict+load ops per second).
- When memory bandwidth >85 GB/s, pageback latency increases non-linearly and causes the reward signal to be delayed, which destabilizes gradient updates.

Actionable mitigations tried in-lab:
1) Reward smoothing: add a decay penalty for re-loads within 10s, reduced oscillation magnitude significantly (peak bandwidth down ~13% on surge runs).
2) Eviction hysteresis: prevent the agent from touching the same keyset for 2s after eviction (simple cooldown). Eliminated repeated churn on several hosts but increased avg resident set age.
3) Centralized periodic regularization: occasionally pull a small batch of cross-host experiences to align policies; reduced inter-host variance in behavior.
4) Constraint layer: hard cap on per-epoch evict+load ops per host to bound bandwidth; prevents worst-case spikes but increases baseline pagebacks marginally.

Risks and trade-offs:
- Complexity: Adds more moving parts to the runtime path and requires robust telemetry to debug training-induced regressions.
- Safety: Online learning in prod could accidentally learn pathological behaviors without safe guards (we need kill-switch and conservative default fallback).
- Operational cost: extra CPU cycles and storage for logs; some extra memory jitter during warmup.

Open questions / experiments to run next:
- Can we switch to an actor-critic variant with critic trained offline from historical traces? Might provide a smoother reward baseline and fewer online oscillations.
- Test larger reward windows (20–60s) and measure impact on useful-reuse vs bandwidth. We need to quantify cost of longer conservatism (potentially evicting fewer items).
- Evaluate per-tenant vs pooled policies: do tenant-aware policies consistently win on tail SLOs for big customers?
- Better features: include short-term sequence-length histogram per-request bucket and host-level BW gradient as input to avoid sudden surprising actions.

Implementation notes and TODOs:
- PR #289 adds decision telemetry and proto agent. Need to harden serialization and ensure logs include host-clock sync timestamping (current logs use monotonic TS; makes cross-host replay awkward).
- Add circuit-breaker: if host-level pageback rate > X for Y seconds, force agent to freeze and fallback to baseline LRU-priority for 30s.
- Create joinable dashboard: reuse-rate, pagebacks/sec, host BW, p99 token latency correlated to agent action rate. Liam to add panels (ENG-1287).

Conclusion (interim):
Prototype shows promise: measurable reuse gains and lower average pageback in steady regimes. Main failure mode is oscillation during bursty workloads causing transient bandwidth amplification and tail latency spikes. Short-term mitigations (reward smoothing, hysteresis, cross-host regularization) reduce but do not eliminate the issue. Next steps focus on safer training (offline critic or larger windows), stronger circuit-breakers, and tenant-aware features.

Appendix: quick numbers table (avg across hosts) - from run ids: run-2025-11-18-a (baseline) and run-2025-11-18-b (RL):
- Baseline reuse: 72.3% | RL reuse: 78.9%
- Baseline pagebacks/sec: 2.2 | RL: 1.6
- Baseline p99 token latency: 161ms | RL: 150ms
Note: these are staging microbench numbers, not yet validated in production.

Notes-to-self:
- Keep conservative rollout: canary 5 hosts, monitor spike detectors on BW and pagebacks.
- Pair with release engineering for kill-switch hook in agent config.
- Share short writeup for product (Optimize) to see if this direction aligns with cost/performance story.
